topics: 🕊️ Met Mitzva — 'sit and refrain' is different: no general rule that dignity overrides Torah
✨ Why No Miracles for Us? — Rav Pappa and Abaye: earlier generations sacrificed themselves for God's name
🧵 Rav Adda bar Ahava — tore a kilayim garment off a woman who turned out not to be Jewish: 400 zuz
👁️ Joseph and the Evil Eye — Rabbi Yoḥanan at the immersion gates; 'alei ayin' read as 'olei ayin'
👩 Women, Slaves, and Minors — exempt from Shema and tefillin; obligated in prayer, mezuza, and Grace
🍞 Kiddush and Birkat HaMazon — 'Remember' and 'Observe'; can a woman fulfill others' obligation?
💭 Contemplation vs. Speech — the ba'al keri contemplates Shema: Ravina and Rav Ḥisda disagree

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Women's Mitzvot and the Ba'al Keri
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 20a–20b
overview.hebrewSource: נָשִׁים וַעֲבָדִים וּקְטַנִּים פְּטוּרִין מִקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּמִן הַתְּפִילִּין, וְחַיָּיבִין בִּתְפִלָּה וּבִמְזוּזָה וּבְבִרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes the human-dignity discussion: the Nazirite may bury a met mitzva, but only because 'sit and refrain from action' is different. Rav Pappa asks Abaye why miracles happened for earlier generations and not for us; the answer is self-sacrifice for God's name, illustrated by Rav Adda bar Ahava, Rav Giddel, and Rabbi Yoḥanan. A new mishna then exempts women, slaves, and minors from Shema and tefillin but obligates them in prayer, mezuza, and Grace after Meals. The Gemara explains why each ruling needed stating, debates whether women's kiddush and Grace are Torah law, and finally opens the laws of the ba'al keri: does contemplation count as speech?

slides.title: ✨ Why Did Miracles Happen for Them and Not for Us?
slides.subtitle: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye, and three stories of the earlier generations

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa
lines.text: In Rav Yehuda's day all their learning was Nezikin, while we learn all six orders — thirteen versions of Okatzin! Yet when Rav Yehuda removed one shoe, rain fell; we cry out and no one notices.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: The earlier generations gave their lives for the sanctification of God's name (קְדוּשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם); we do not.

lines.speaker: Story 1
lines.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava saw a woman in the market wearing a karbalta of kilayim. Thinking she was Jewish, he tore it off her. She was not — he was fined 400 zuz. 'What is your name?' 'Matun.' 'Matun, matun — worth 400 zuz.'

lines.speaker: Story 2
lines.text: Rav Giddel sat at the immersion gates instructing women how to immerse. 'Aren't you afraid of the evil inclination?' 'They are like white geese to me.'

lines.speaker: Story 3
lines.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan sat there so women would see him and bear beautiful children. 'Aren't you afraid of the evil eye?' 'I descend from Joseph, over whom the evil eye has no dominion.'

callout.label: Joseph's immunity:
callout.text: Rabbi Abbahu: read עֲלֵי עָיִן (Genesis 49:22) as עוֹלֵי עָיִן, 'above the eye'. Rabbi Yosei b. Rabbi Ḥanina: 'may they multiply like fish' (Genesis 48:16) — water covers fish, so the evil eye cannot see them. Or: an eye that refused to feast on what was not his is immune to the evil eye.

slides.title: 👩 The Mishna's Five Rulings — Why Each Needed Saying
slides.subtitle: Women, slaves, and minors: each 'obvious' ruling blocks a wrong inference
rows: It contains acceptance of the yoke of Heaven — you might think women are obligated anyway
Tefillin is juxtaposed to mezuza (Deut. 6:8–9) — you might equate them
It is a plea for mercy; but 'evening, morning, and afternoon' (Psalms 55:18) could make it look time-bound
Mezuza is juxtaposed to Torah study (Deut. 11:19–20), from which women are exempt
'Meat in the evening and bread in the morning' (Exodus 16:8) could make it look time-bound

callout.label: The rule:
callout.text: מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁהַזְּמַן גְּרָמָא — women are exempt from any positive mitzva caused by time. Shema is bound to morning and evening; tefillin to weekdays and daytime.

slides.title: 🍷 Are Women Obligated in Kiddush by Torah Law?
slides.subtitle: Rav Adda bar Ahava's ruling and Rava's derivation

nodes.content: 📜 Rav Adda bar Ahava: women are obligated in kiddush of Shabbat by Torah law
❓ Why? Kiddush is a time-bound positive mitzva, and women are exempt from those!

columns.label: Rava's rejection
columns.content: But he said 'by Torah law'! And if so, obligate them rabbinically in every time-bound mitzva

nodes.content: ✅ Rava: זָכוֹר וְשָׁמוֹר — 'Remember' (Exodus 20:8) and 'Observe' (Deut. 5:12). Whoever is included in observing Shabbat is included in remembering it. Women must observe, so they must remember (kiddush)

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: The two versions of the Ten Commandments are read as one unit: the prohibitions (Observe) and the positive mitzva (Remember) share the same set of obligated people.

slides.title: 🍞 Can a Woman Recite Grace on Behalf of Others?
slides.subtitle: Ravina asks Rava: is women's Birkat HaMazon from the Torah or the Rabbis?

steps.content: 1️⃣ The practical difference: one obligated only rabbinically cannot fulfill the obligation of one obligated by Torah law — כׇּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּיָּיב בַּדָּבָר אֵינוֹ מוֹצִיא אֶת הָרַבִּים
2️⃣ Proof attempt: a baraita says a son may bless for his father, a slave for his master, a woman for her husband — though 'may a curse come to a man whose wife and children bless for him'
3️⃣ If women's obligation were rabbinic, how could she fulfill her husband's Torah obligation? So it must be Torah law
4️⃣ Rejected: by that logic a minor is Torah-obligated too! Rather, the father ate only a rabbinic measure (not to satiety), so rabbinic fulfills rabbinic. The question stands

callout.label: Aggada:
callout.text: Rav Avira (in the name of Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Asi): the angels asked how God 'shows favor' to Israel (Numbers 6:26) when He 'favors no one' (Deut. 10:17). God answered: I wrote 'you shall eat and be satisfied and bless' (Deut. 8:10), yet they are exacting with themselves to bless even over an olive-bulk or an egg-bulk.

slides.title: 💭 Is Contemplation Like Speech?
slides.subtitle: The mishna: a ba'al keri contemplates Shema in his heart without blessings; blesses after food but not before

boxes.title: Ravina: הִרְהוּר כְּדִבּוּר דָּמֵי
items: Otherwise, why would the ba'al keri contemplate at all?
Then why not say it aloud? 'As we found at Sinai' — those impure had to immerse before hearing the spoken Torah

boxes.title: Rav Ḥisda: לָאו כְּדִבּוּר דָּמֵי
items: If it were, he should simply utter the words with his lips
Then why contemplate? Rabbi Elazar: so he is not sitting idle while everyone else recites Shema

boxes.title: Why Shema specifically?
items: Let him study a different chapter instead!
Rav Adda bar Ahava: one should engage in the matter the community is engaged in
Rabbi Yehuda in the mishna: he blesses both before and after

callout.label: Background:
callout.text: Ezra decreed that one impure from a seminal emission may not engage in Torah until he immerses. The mishna allows blessing after food (Torah law) but not before (rabbinic law).

summary.principle: Obligation follows category, not importance: women are exempt from time-bound positive mitzvot yet obligated in prayer, mezuza, Grace, and kiddush; and the Gemara carefully tracks which obligations are Torah law and which are rabbinic.

flowSteps.content: 🕊️ Met mitzva overrides the Nazirite's purity only because 'sit and refrain' is different — no general rule that dignity beats Torah
✨ Earlier generations merited miracles through self-sacrifice for God's name: Rav Adda's 400 zuz, Rav Giddel, Rabbi Yoḥanan and Joseph's immunity to the evil eye
👩 Mishna: women, slaves, minors exempt from Shema and tefillin (time-bound); obligated in prayer (mercy), mezuza, and Grace

columns.content: 🍞 Grace: Torah or rabbinic? Determines whether she can fulfill others' obligation — unresolved

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: The ba'al keri contemplates Shema — whether contemplation equals speech (Ravina) or he simply joins the community's activity (Rav Ḥisda), he is not left idle

quiz.q: Why can't a general principle that human dignity overrides Torah law be derived from the Nazirite burying a met mitzva?
o: Because the Nazirite is not bound by purity laws
Because a case of 'sit and refrain from action' is different — he does not actively violate a mitzva
Because burial of a met mitzva is only rabbinic
Because the Nazirite's relatives may bury the body instead
quiz.e: Engaging in the burial does not directly contravene a mitzva; it only renders him unable to fulfill one. Such a shev ve'al ta'aseh case cannot teach that dignity overrides an active prohibition.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, why did miracles occur for the earlier generations but not for Rav Pappa's generation?
o: Because they studied all six orders of the Mishna
Because they learned thirteen versions of Okatzin
Because they were wholly devoted to sanctifying God's name, and we are not
Because they fasted more often for rain
quiz.e: Rav Pappa noted that his generation learned far more than Rav Yehuda's, yet Rav Yehuda's removing one shoe brought rain. Abaye answered that the earlier generations were dedicated to sanctifying God's name.

quiz.q: Why did the mishna need to state that women are exempt from Shema if it is obviously a time-bound positive mitzva?
o: Because Shema is juxtaposed to mezuza
Because Shema contains acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, so one might think women are obligated regardless
Because women were obligated in Shema by an earlier decree
Because minors are obligated in Shema
quiz.e: The Gemara says: lest you say that since Shema includes acceptance of the kingdom of Heaven women should be obligated, the mishna teaches that they are nevertheless exempt.

quiz.q: How does Rava derive that women are obligated in kiddush by Torah law?
o: From the juxtaposition of kiddush and mezuza
From 'evening, morning, and afternoon' in Psalms
From 'Remember' and 'Observe': whoever is included in observing Shabbat is included in remembering it
From the fact that women are obligated in prayer
quiz.e: Rava rejected Abaye's claim that it is only rabbinic and derived it from the two versions of the commandment (Exodus 20:8 and Deuteronomy 5:12).

quiz.q: How does the Gemara refute the proof from 'a son may bless for his father' that women's Grace after Meals is Torah law?
o: A minor is certainly not Torah-obligated, so the baraita must refer to a father who ate only a rabbinic measure
The baraita is only a curse, not a halakha
The son in the baraita is an adult
Women are never mentioned in the baraita
quiz.e: Since a minor is exempt by Torah law yet the baraita lets him bless for his father, the father must have eaten less than satiety, an amount obligating Grace only rabbinically — so rabbinic fulfills rabbinic, and the proof collapses.
